name: Margaret Ellison
presenting_complaint: Sudden severe pain and blurred vision in the right eye with haloes and vomiting

medical_history.social: Retired teacher. Non-smoker. Symptoms began while watching a movie in a dark cinema.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 63-year-old woman presents with a 3-hour history of sudden severe right eye pain, blurred vision and coloured haloes around lights that began in a dark cinema. She is nauseated and has vomited twice. On examination the right eye is red, the cornea looks hazy and the pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. The globe feels hard to palpation. She reports the vision is now markedly reduced.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Speed of onset and character of pain: sudden, severe, unilateral ocular/peri-orbital pain
Visual symptoms: blurred/reduced vision and coloured haloes around lights
Precipitant: onset in dim light (cinema) causing pupil dilatation; ask about anticholinergics/sympathomimetics
Associated systemic symptoms: nausea, vomiting, headache
Risk factors: hypermetropia/long-sightedness, older age, female sex, family history of glaucoma, Asian ethnicity
Key negatives to screen: no trauma, no contact lens use, no discharge; screen for GCA features (jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal headache) and amaurosis
Past ocular history and prior similar episodes
objective: ALWAYS test and record visual acuity in both eyes — reduced acuity in the affected right eye
Inspect: circumcorneal (ciliary) injection, hazy/cloudy oedematous cornea
Palpation: globe feels hard/stony (raised intraocular pressure); measure IOP if able (markedly elevated, often greater than 40 mmHg)
Assess for relative afferent pupillary defect and fundoscopy where possible
Vital signs including BP; document nausea/vomiting
assessment: Primary diagnosis: Acute angle-closure glaucoma of the right eye — a sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency
Document supporting features: hard red eye, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes, precipitated by dim light in a hypermetrope

Consider and exclude other sight-threatening causes of acute red/painful eye: anterior uveitis/iritis, orbital cellulitis, and, for sudden painless loss, central retinal artery occlusion and giant cell arteritis
Recognise vision loss is time-critical — irreversible optic nerve damage without urgent IOP reduction
plan: Urgent (emergency) ophthalmology referral immediately by phone with a documented time — do not wait for the morning clinic
Commence IOP-lowering therapy while awaiting ophthalmology: topical timolol, apraclonidine/brimonidine and pilocarpine 2%, plus topical steroid as directed
Systemic IOP reduction: acetazolamide 500 mg IV/PO (check for sulfonamide allergy and contraindications)
Analgesia and antiemetic for pain and vomiting; lie patient supine (face up) to help the lens fall back
Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy — arranged by ophthalmology; prophylactic iridotomy to the fellow eye
Check for and exclude giant cell arteritis if any suggestive features (ESR/CRP, temporal artery symptoms) given age
Serial IOP and visual acuity monitoring; clear safety-netting and documented disposition to eye unit

critical_errors: Failing to exclude/identify a vision-threatening cause (acute angle-closure glaucoma, GCA, CRAO, orbital cellulitis) and treating as benign conjunctivitis
Not testing and recording visual acuity in a painful red eye
Delaying urgent ophthalmology referral and IOP-lowering treatment (no documented referral or timing) — allowing irreversible vision loss
Instilling a mydriatic/dilating drop, which worsens angle closure
must_not_miss: Acute angle-closure glaucoma recognised and IOP-lowering treatment started urgently
Urgent same-hour ophthalmology referral documented with a time
Other sight-threatening causes (GCA, CRAO, orbital cellulitis, anterior uveitis) explicitly considered
